title: Private deployments: VPC & on‑prem deployment reference + day‑2 ops, upgrade and rollback
author: Alyssa Chen
body:
Overview

This document is a single consolidated reference for Redwood Private deployments (VPC and on‑prem packaging), reference architectures, day‑2 operations, and the supported upgrade & rollback procedures. It is intended for SREs, field engineers, and Solutions Engineering who lead customer deployments and post‑go‑live operations.

Scope

- Supported deployment modes: VPC (customer cloud) and fully on‑prem (air‑gapped or private data center)
- Focus areas: reference architectures, packaging details, deployment checklist, day‑2 runbook, upgrade/rollback playbooks, and a concise customer requirements library
- Out of scope: internal hosted (SaaS) product operational runbooks (see eng-sre runbooks)

Owners & contacts

- Doc owner: Alyssa Chen (eng-private-deployments)
- Primary oncall for deploys: Private Deployments Pager (team schedule)
- Escalation: Tier 2 SWE lead (Diego Martinez) -> Head of Private Deployments (Priya Rao)

High level reference architectures

1) VPC (customer cloud) reference architecture

- Description: Redwood control plane (hosted) + customer VPC data plane. Network traffic is managed with customer NAT/IGW, private routes to Redwood peering/VPN, and optional private endpoints.
- Components:
  - Customer VPC with dedicated subnets: control-plane-egress, app-subnets, storage-subnets
  - Bastion / jump host for admin access (restricted to customer IPs)
  - Private NLB/ALB in front of inference workers for internal traffic
  - Managed object store (S3/GCS) or on‑prem NFS for model assets and snapshots
  - KMS integration: customer KMS or HSM for key wrapping
- Recommended sizing (example):
  - Small: 4x GPU nodes (A100/RTX equivalent), 2x CPU control-plane, 1x metadata DB (db.t3.medium or equivalent managed)
  - Medium: 16x GPU nodes + HA control-plane (2x), 2x metadata DB (primary+hot standby)
  - Network: 10Gbps private connectivity between nodes recommended for low-latency KV cache sync

2) On‑prem / air‑gapped reference architecture

- Description: All components run in customer datacenter. Control plane optionally operated by Redwood as a lightweight control endpoint inside customer network or fully air‑gapped with offline operator tooling.
- Components:
  - Orchestration: Kubernetes (1.25+ supported) or VMware/vSphere options (documented packaging)
  - Storage: Local NVMe for model cache, SAN/NAS for persistent model storage
  - Networking: Private L2/L3 segmentation, multicast disabled, strict egress rules for air‑gapped installs
  - Hardware: GPU nodes with direct NVLink where latency sensitive (recommendation depends on model size)

Packaging & distribution options

- Kubernetes Helm chart (recommended): supports VPC & on‑prem, parameterized values.yaml for networking, storage, and quantization profiles
- OVA / VM images: used for customers without Kubernetes; images include preinstalled runtime and supervisor agent
- Air‑gapped bundle: tarball with container images, packages, migration tools, and an offline installer script

Prerequisites (customer checklist)

1) Networking & security
  - BGP or static routes configured for Redwood peering (if applicable)
  - Required ports open between control plane and data plane: 443 (control), 8443 (metrics), 50051 (gRPC internal) — confirm with security team
  - DNS entries for internal load balancers and operator endpoints
  - Private container registry accessible (for on‑prem) or registry bridge configured

2) Identity & key management
  - Customer KMS access or agreed key escrow process for on‑prem installs
  - SSO/OIDC SAML integration details for RBAC and admin console access

3) Storage & compute
  - Persistent storage for model artifacts (S3/GCS or NFS/CIFS) with >= 3x replicas for durability recommendations
  - GPU node specifications, NVMe sizing guidance and minimum IO benchmarks

Deployment procedure (VPC & on‑prem common flow)

Pre‑deployment (1–3 days)
1. Confirm customer requirements from the Customer Requirements Library (see below).
2. Exchange network diagrams and agree maintenance windows.
3. Validate access: CI/CD runner to private registry, KMS credentials, jump host access.
4. Generate environment-specific values.yaml from template.

Deployment steps (Kubernetes/Helm example)
1. Provision base infra (VPC subnets / VLANs, storage backends, DNS).
2. Push required container images to customer registry (air‑gapped: use offline bundle).
3. Apply Helm chart: helm upgrade --install redwood-private ./chart -f values.yaml --namespace redwood
4. Validate pods: kubectl get pods -n redwood (expect control-plane, runtime-worker, node-agent, exporter)
5. Run smoke tests: latency test suite, model load test, KV cache warmup
6. Perform initial load test (thin load) and confirm SLOs
7. Hand over runbook and monitoring dashboards to customer SREs

Post‑deployment validation checklist

- All control-plane APIs Healthy (200 OK health endpoints)
- Model load times within expected baseline (+/- 10%)
- KV cache hit rate > 70% for warm traffic patterns
- Prometheus metrics scraped and visible in Grafana dashboards

Day‑2 operations (runbook highlights)

Monitoring & alerting
- Default SLOs:
  - 99th percentile generation latency (short prompts): target <= 250ms for lightweight configs
  - Model load success rate: >= 99.9% over 24h
  - Cluster GPU utilization: alert on sustained >85% for 10m
- Key alerts: control-plane unhealthy, worker crashloop, image pull errors, disk pressure on model storage, KMS access failures

Common day‑2 tasks
1. Scaling GPUs: adjust node pool size and scale runtime-workers via autoscaler; perform canary capacity check before opening traffic.
2. Certificate rotation: follow the certificate rotation playbook (cron job + rolling restart in values.yaml).
3. Model management: upload new model artifact to object store, update model manifest, and trigger model-onboard job.
4. Backups: nightly snapshot of metadata DB + daily backup of model manifests. Verify restore at least quarterly.

Maintenance windows & patching
- Recommended cadence: monthly minor patches, quarterly kernel/GPU driver updates (schedule with customer).
- Rolling upgrade pattern: drain -> patch -> uncordon per node (max 10% concurrent drain for production clusters).

Upgrade procedure (minor and major)

Minor upgrades (patches, config changes)
1. Create a release branch and artifact bundle.
2. Run canary on non‑prod environment mirrored to customer configuration.
3. Announce maintenance window and create incident bridge.
4. Apply Helm upgrade with --timeout and probe timeouts tuned.
5. Validate smoke tests and metrics for 30 minutes before progressing.

Major upgrades (runtime / schema / model format changes)
1. Read the upgrade notes in the release manifest. Confirm compatibility of model artifacts and KV cache formats.
2. Execute staged rollout: control-plane first (HA), then canary data-plane nodes, then full fleet.
3. If the release includes irreversible DB migrations, ensure backup and offline migration plan.

Rollback procedure (fast rollback / safe rollback)

Fast rollback (post-failure within maintenance window)
1. Immediately pause rollout and mark circuit-breaker to stop new traffic.
2. Helm rollback: helm rollback redwood <previous-revision> -n redwood
3. Restart baseline smoke tests and monitor SLOs for 30 minutes.
4. If rollback fails, escalate to engineering lead and prepare DB restore.

Safe rollback (if DB schema changed)
1. Restore metadata DB snapshot taken pre-upgrade to a staging environment and validate application behavior.
2. Coordinate with customer to revert client-side caches or API tokens if necessary.
3. Reconcile any model manifest changes with the object store.

Customer requirements library (summary table)

- Networking: BGP or static routes, NAT/IGW details, port matrix (443, 8443, 50051), private DNS
- Identity: SAML/OIDC issuer URL, admin users list, group mappings for RBAC
- Keys & secrets: KMS ARN / endpoint, key access policies, HSM constraints if required
- Storage: object store endpoint, IAM/credentials pattern, minimum IOPS for NVMe, retention policy
- Compute: GPU type, per‑node memory, NIC speed, disk layout (root/ephemeral/nvme)
- Compliance: data residency region, encryption-at-rest requirements, audit logging retention

(For a printable checklist, see appendix: customer-requirements-checklist table snippet.)

Troubleshooting & known issues

- Symptom: slow model load times
  - Check: network egress bandwidth, NVMe IO wait, model shard placement
  - Mitigation: increase model cache size, pre-warm caches, optimize model shard topology

- Symptom: repeated image pull errors in on‑prem installs
  - Check: registry credentials, image manifest compatibility, proxy settings
  - Mitigation: re-push images, confirm registry TLS settings, inspect kubelet logs

Operational playbook snippet: incident response for worker OOMs
1. Add worker node to maintenance (cordon + drain).
2. Capture logs: kubectl logs <pod> --previous and /var/log/syslog on host.
3. Inspect pod resource requests & limits; consider increasing ephemeral storage or memory limits for the pod type.
4. Redeploy with adjusted resources in a canary and monitor 15m before resuming traffic.

Appendix: example values.yaml snippets

# Networking and registry examples
registry:
  url: "https://registry.internal.example.com"
  username: "<redacted>"
  pullPolicy: IfNotPresent

networking:
  ingressClass: internal
  internalPorts:
    control: 443
    metrics: 8443
    grpc: 50051

# Model manifest example (JSON stored in object store)
model_manifest: |
  {
    "model": "redwood/open-7b",
    "version": "2025-10-01",
    "shards": 4,
    "quantization": "int8"
  }

Recovery validation checklist

- Confirm metadata DB restore success with sample query results.
- Load one production model and validate inference latency and correctness.
- Confirm all alerting and dashboard links are operational.
